title: Inside Southeast Asia's Run Club Culture
seo_title: Inside Southeast Asia's Run Club Culture
meta_description: 186 running clubs and 17 coaches across 19 Southeast Asian cities: where they meet, when they run, what they cost, and how to join one.
dek: From Jakarta's Car Free Day crews to Bangkok's park loop after dark, the run club is one of the most visible parts of Southeast Asia's city running. The format started here, and the Run SEA clubs directory now counts 186 clubs across 19 cities.

sections.heading: A format with regional roots
paragraphs: The group run built as much around company as training isn't new to this region. The Hash House Harriers began in Kuala Lumpur in December 1938, when British expatriates started meeting on Friday evenings for a run followed by a drink, and the club still calls itself a drinking club with a running problem[1]. The second chapter opened in Singapore in 1962, and the format has since spread to about 1,500 chapters worldwide[1].

The hash is still part of the scene. The Run SEA directory lists 42 hash chapters in 12 of its 19 cities, from Bangkok and Singapore, with seven each, to single kennels in Hanoi, Cebu and Phnom Penh[3]. Kuching's hash leads the organising committee for Interhash 2028, the worldwide hash gathering, which the city hosts from 14 to 16 July 2028[3]. The road clubs and crews that now draw the biggest crowds are a more running-focused generation, but the idea is the same: the run gets people out the door, and what happens around it keeps them coming back.

sections.heading: What the directory counts
paragraphs: The Run SEA clubs directory at runsea.run/clubs/ lists 186 clubs and 17 coaches across 19 cities in seven countries, each with where and when it meets and what it costs[3]. Indonesia has the most after five new cities were added: 52 clubs and 7 coaches across Jakarta (13 clubs), Yogyakarta (11), Bandung (9), Medan (6), Bali (5), Surabaya (5) and Semarang (3). Singapore has 36 clubs and 4 coaches. Thailand has 33 clubs (Bangkok 19, Chiang Mai 9, Phuket 5), and Malaysia 31 (Kuala Lumpur 18, Penang 8, Kuching 5) with one coach. The Philippines (Manila 9, Cebu 5) and Vietnam (Hanoi 7, Ho Chi Minh City 7) have 14 each, and Phnom Penh has 6[3].

Most are free. Of the clubs that state a cost, 56 are free and 26 charge, most of them hash chapters collecting a run fee for food, drinks or a bus to the trail[3]. Seventeen are brand clubs run by sportswear or watch companies, including adidas, ASICS, PUMA and Garmin, which are usually free but sometimes cap places and ask you to sign up for each session.

sections.heading: Real clubs, city by city
paragraphs: In Jakarta, Indo Runners, founded in 2009, has grown into a national community with chapters in Bali, Bandung, Surabaya and Yogyakarta[3]. Smaller crews like We Run Jakarta, started in 2016 by friends who kept meeting at races around Senayan, run three sessions a week from fixed points including FX Sudirman and the GBK east car park[2]. In Manila, most group runs start in the business districts: the Ayala Triangle and Rockwell in Makati, High Street in BGC and UP Diliman in Quezon City, with clubs such as RWP Run Club and runnr club alongside two long-running hash kennels[3].

Bangkok's runs centre on Lumpini Park and Benjakitti Park, which an elevated walkway joins into a traffic-free loop of about 10 km; Lumpini's evening runs set off after the 6pm national anthem[3]. Kuala Lumpur's clubs mostly run after dark on weeknights, starting between 7:30pm and 9pm, or at dawn at weekends, from places such as KLCC Park, Desa ParkCity and Bukit Jalil. Singapore's 36 clubs meet mostly on weekday evenings between about 6.30pm and 7.45pm or early on weekend mornings, around Marina Bay, the Kallang, East Coast Park and public stadium tracks. In Hanoi, Chay365 has held a Saturday dawn long run at Hoan Kiem Lake for more than 225 weeks[3].

sections.heading: Parks, lakes and car-free mornings
paragraphs: Because many city streets are hard to run on for much of the day, a few traffic-free spaces take a large share of each city's runners. In Indonesia that often means Car Free Day. On Sunday mornings Jakarta closes Jalan Sudirman to traffic, and community runs there start as early as 5:30am. Surabaya keeps the main lane of Jalan Raya Darmo clear, Semarang closes the roads around Simpang Lima from about 6am, and Medan opens the area around Lapangan Merdeka to runners from 6am[3].

Elsewhere the hub is a park, a lake or a business-district loop. Cebu's everyday running happens on the roughly 1.2 km loop around Cebu IT Park, busy at 5am and 6pm on weekdays. Hanoi's groups gather around lakes such as Hoan Kiem and Den Lu, much of Ho Chi Minh City's group running happens in the Sala area of Thu Thiem, and Penang's clubs run the waterfronts at Tanjung Tokong, Q1 and Gurney Bay from about 8:30pm[3].

The timing follows the heat. In city after city in the directory, road clubs meet before about 7am or after sunset, and the long run moves to a weekend dawn, when roads are quietest; hash runs are the exception, often setting off in the late afternoon[3]. The same pressures explain why the region's races start so early: see runsea.run/articles/why-southeast-asia-races-start-before-dawn/.

sections.heading: Why the format took off here
paragraphs: Safety in numbers matters in cities where the best running weather falls before sunrise or after dark: a group moving together through a park at 5am or 9pm is safer than a runner alone. Fixed meeting points and known routes are also useful in dense, traffic-heavy cities, where finding a good place to run is half the problem.

Social media has helped spread the format: for 102 of the 186 clubs in the directory, the main link is an Instagram account, and many use WhatsApp, Telegram, Zalo or Strava groups for the details[3]. What keeps people coming back is simpler: the run gets someone out of the door, and the coffee or breakfast afterwards builds the habit of returning the next week.

sections.heading: How to find and join one
paragraphs: Start with the city page in the directory, then check the club's own latest post before you go, because many crews change their start point each week and some post only a few days ahead[3]. Brand clubs and run-specialty stores are an easy first step: most run a free weekly session open to any pace. In cities such as Medan, where several clubs post only occasionally, message the club before your first run.

For a first visit, pick a session advertised as beginner-friendly or no-drop, meaning nobody is left behind, rather than a club's tempo or interval night. Most established clubs are used to newcomers arriving alone, and the second visit is far easier than the first.

sources.label: Run SEA clubs directory (186 clubs and 17 coaches in 19 cities, checked Nov 2026)

faqs.question: Are Southeast Asia's run clubs a new phenomenon?
faqs.answer: The current wave of crews is recent, but the format has deep roots here. The Hash House Harriers began in Kuala Lumpur in 1938 and reached Singapore in 1962, and now has about 1,500 chapters worldwide. The Run SEA directory still lists 42 hash chapters across 12 Southeast Asian cities, alongside the newer road clubs and crews.

faqs.question: How do I find a run club in a Southeast Asian city?
faqs.answer: Start with the city's page in the Run SEA clubs directory at runsea.run/clubs/, which lists 186 clubs across 19 cities with meeting points, times and costs. Then check the club's latest Instagram post before going, since many crews change their start point weekly and confirm details in WhatsApp or Telegram groups.

faqs.question: Do run clubs in Southeast Asia charge a fee?
faqs.answer: Most don't. Of the clubs in the Run SEA directory that state a cost, 56 are free and 26 charge, and most of those charging are hash chapters collecting a run fee for food, drinks or transport. Brand clubs are usually free but may cap places and ask you to sign up for each session.
